ep-meca-001.question: In a ventricular myocyte, which current is responsible for the rapid depolarisation (phase 0) of the action potential?
options: The fast inward sodium current, INa
The inward rectifier potassium current, IK1
commentaires: Correct: abrupt opening of Nav1.5 channels (INa) generates phase 0 in fast-response cells; its upstroke velocity determines conduction velocity.
Incorrect: IK1 maintains the resting potential (phase 4) and terminal repolarisation; it does not depolarise the cell.
Incorrect: ICaL carries phase 0 in nodal cells, but in ventricular myocardium it contributes mainly to the plateau (phase 2).
Incorrect: If contributes to diastolic depolarisation in automatic cells, not to phase 0 in working myocardium.
ep-meca-001.explication: Phase 0 of the action potential in "fast-response" cells (atrial and ventricular myocardium, Purkinje fibres) results from abrupt opening of Nav1.5 sodium channels (SCN5A gene): this is INa. Its upstroke velocity (dV/dt max) determines conduction velocity, which explains the effect of class I antiarrhythmic drugs, which block it and widen the QRS. In these cells, ICaL contributes mainly to the plateau (phase 2). IK1 maintains the resting potential (phase 4), and If contributes to diastolic depolarisation in automatic cells. The pitfall is confusion with nodal cells, whose phase 0 is calcium-dependent.
ep-meca-001.aRetenir: Phase 0 in ventricular myocardium is sodium-dependent (INa, Nav1.5) and determines conduction velocity.

ep-meca-002.question: Which ionic current, the target of ivabradine, contributes to slow diastolic depolarisation (phase 4) in sinus node cells?
commentaires: Incorrect: IKr is a repolarising current (phase 3) and the target of class III antiarrhythmic drugs.
Incorrect: INaL is a late sodium current active during the plateau, targeted by ranolazine, not ivabradine.
Incorrect: Ito is an outward current responsible for early repolarisation (phase 1).
Correct: If, an inward current activated by hyperpolarisation and carried by HCN4, generates the sinus diastolic slope; ivabradine blocks it.
ep-meca-002.explication: Sinus node automaticity relies on spontaneous diastolic depolarisation during phase 4. The If current, carried by HCN channels (mainly HCN4), is an inward current activated by hyperpolarisation; it is modulated by cAMP, and therefore by the autonomic nervous system. Ivabradine blocks it selectively and slows the sinus rate without any inotropic effect. Other mechanisms also contribute (T- and L-type calcium currents, and the Na/Ca exchanger activated by calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum: the "calcium clock"). IKr and Ito are repolarising currents; INaL is a late sodium current active during the plateau.
ep-meca-002.aRetenir: If (HCN4) is the main current underlying the sinus diastolic slope and is the target of ivabradine.

ep-meca-003.question: True or false: phase 0 of the action potential in sinus node and atrioventricular node cells depends mainly on the L-type calcium current (ICaL).
commentaires: Correct: the less negative diastolic potential (about −60 mV) inactivates sodium channels; nodal phase 0 is carried by ICaL.
Incorrect: the statement is true; it is working myocardium, not nodal tissue, whose phase 0 depends on the fast sodium current.
ep-meca-003.explication: This is true. Nodal cells (sinus node, compact AV node) are "slow-response" cells: their diastolic potential is less negative (about −60 mV), which inactivates most sodium channels. Their phase 0 depends on the L-type calcium current (ICaL), hence slow depolarisation and slow conduction. This explains why the AV node is sensitive to calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) and adenosine, and relatively insensitive to class I antiarrhythmic drugs. The pitfall is to apply to nodal tissue the physiology of working myocardium, whose phase 0 is sodium-dependent.
ep-meca-003.aRetenir: In nodal tissue, phase 0 is calcium-dependent (ICaL), hence the slow, decremental conduction of the AV node.

ep-meca-004.question: Most non-cardiac drugs that prolong the QT interval (macrolides, some antipsychotics, antihistamines, etc.) do so by blocking which current?
commentaires: Incorrect: IKs is rarely a drug target; loss-of-function mutations cause long QT type 1.
Correct: the large inner cavity of the hERG channel binds a great many molecules; this is the almost universal mechanism of acquired long QT.
Incorrect: IK1 stabilises the resting potential; drug-induced block of IK1 is not the usual mechanism of QT prolongation.
Incorrect: blocking INa widens the QRS and, if anything, tends to shorten repolarisation.
ep-meca-004.explication: Repolarisation (phase 3) relies mainly on two delayed rectifier potassium currents: IKr (rapid) and IKs (slow). The hERG channel, which carries IKr, has a large inner cavity that readily binds many molecules: this is the almost universal mechanism of acquired QT prolongation and drug-induced torsades de pointes. Loss-of-function mutations in KCNH2 cause long QT type 2, and those in KCNQ1 (IKs) type 1. IK1 stabilises the resting potential and terminal repolarisation; drug-induced block of IK1 is not the usual mechanism. An INa blocker tends, if anything, to shorten repolarisation and widens the QRS.
ep-meca-004.aRetenir: Drug-induced acquired long QT almost always involves IKr (hERG) block.

ep-meca-005.question: Which of the following properties characterise the "slow-response" tissue of the atrioventricular node? (multiple answers)
options: Decremental conduction: conduction time lengthens as the coupling interval shortens
Refractoriness that outlasts the end of repolarisation (post-repolarisation refractoriness)
High sensitivity to class I antiarrhythmic drugs, which markedly prolong the AH interval
An effective refractory period that shortens markedly as rate increases, as in ventricular myocardium
commentaires: Correct: the earlier the premature beat, the longer the AH interval; this filter protects the ventricles from rapid atrial rates.
Correct: nodal refractoriness is time-dependent and outlasts the action potential duration.
Incorrect: as nodal phase 0 is calcium-dependent, the AV node is relatively insensitive to sodium channel blockers; it is, however, very sensitive to calcium channel blockers and adenosine.
Incorrect: the AV nodal ERP tends to lengthen, not shorten, as the basic cycle length shortens.
ep-meca-005.explication: The compact AV node is a tissue whose depolarisation depends on ICaL. It conducts slowly and decrementally: the earlier the premature beat, the longer the AH interval, which protects the ventricles from rapid atrial rates. Its refractoriness is "time-dependent" and outlasts the action potential duration (post-repolarisation refractoriness). It is very sensitive to calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and adenosine, but relatively insensitive to class I antiarrhythmic drugs, which act mainly on fast-response tissue (and tend instead to prolong the HV interval). Moreover, unlike atrial and ventricular myocardium and the His-Purkinje system, its effective refractory period tends to lengthen (rather than shorten) as the basic cycle length shortens.
ep-meca-005.aRetenir: The AV node conducts decrementally, remains refractory after repolarisation, and its ERP lengthens as rate increases.

ep-meca-006.question: A loss-of-function mutation in the SCN5A gene (Nav1.5 sodium channel) is classically associated with:
options: Short QT syndrome due to gain of function
commentaires: Incorrect: long QT type 3 results from gain of function of SCN5A (persistent late sodium current), not loss of function.
Correct: loss of INa function slows conduction (Lenègre disease, progressive conduction disease) and promotes the Brugada phenotype.
Incorrect: CPVT is mainly linked to RYR2 (or CASQ2), genes involved in intracellular calcium handling.
Incorrect: short QT is linked to gain-of-function mutations in potassium channels, not SCN5A.
ep-meca-006.explication: SCN5A encodes the alpha subunit of the cardiac sodium channel. Loss of function reduces INa: slowed conduction (Lenègre disease, progressive conduction disease, sinus node dysfunction) and, through the imbalance of currents at the end of phase 1 in the RV outflow tract epicardium, the Brugada phenotype. Conversely, gain of function (persistent late sodium current) causes long QT type 3. Long QT type 1 is linked to KCNQ1 (IKs), CPVT mainly to RYR2, and short QT to gain-of-function mutations in potassium channels. The classic pitfall is confusing loss and gain of function of SCN5A.
ep-meca-006.aRetenir: SCN5A loss of function = Brugada / conduction disease; gain of function = long QT type 3.

ep-meca-007.question: What are the two electrophysiological conditions essential for the initiation of re-entry?
options: An early afterdepolarisation and a prolonged QT
A long refractory period and rapid conduction
Enhanced automaticity and high vagal tone
commentaires: Incorrect: early afterdepolarisations belong to triggered activity, a mechanism distinct from re-entry.
Incorrect: the opposite is true; long refractoriness and rapid conduction lengthen the wavelength and oppose re-entry.
Correct: unidirectional block in one limb of the circuit, then conduction slow enough to find the point of origin excitable again.
Incorrect: enhanced automaticity is a separate mechanism, and high vagal tone does not create a circuit.
ep-meca-007.explication: Re-entry requires a substrate forming a circuit, with two pathways of differing properties. There must be unidirectional block in one limb (often caused by a premature beat falling within its refractory period), followed by conduction slow enough for the wavefront to return to its point of origin once that tissue has recovered excitability. Long refractoriness and rapid conduction, by contrast, lengthen the wavelength and oppose re-entry. Afterdepolarisations correspond to triggered activity, and enhanced automaticity is a distinct mechanism. This model explains why re-entry can be initiated and terminated by programmed stimulation.
ep-meca-007.aRetenir: Re-entry = circuit + unidirectional block + slow conduction.

ep-meca-008.question: The activation wavelength is the product of conduction velocity and refractory period. Which combination most favours the maintenance of re-entry?
options: Slower conduction and a longer refractory period
Faster conduction and a longer refractory period
Slower conduction and a shorter refractory period
Faster conduction and a shorter refractory period
commentaires: Incorrect: the longer refractoriness offsets the slower conduction; the wavelength is not markedly shortened.
Incorrect: this combination lengthens the wavelength maximally and tends to terminate re-entry.
Correct: slow conduction and short refractoriness give the shortest wavelength, allowing smaller and more numerous circuits.
Incorrect: faster conduction lengthens the wavelength and offsets the shorter refractoriness.
ep-meca-008.explication: Re-entry can only be sustained if the wavelength (conduction velocity × refractory period) is shorter than the circuit length: excitable tissue then remains ahead of the wavefront. Anything that shortens the wavelength (slowed conduction, short refractory period) favours re-entry and allows smaller and more numerous circuits, as in AF with electrical remodelling. Conversely, prolonging the refractory period (class III) lengthens the wavelength and may interrupt the circuit. The pitfall: slowed conduction alone may be proarrhythmic, but it is the combination with short refractoriness that is most unfavourable.
ep-meca-008.aRetenir: Short wavelength (slow conduction + short refractoriness) = re-entry favoured.

ep-meca-009.question: Torsades de pointes occur in a bradycardic woman with a QT of 620 ms on sotalol. Which cellular mechanism triggers the arrhythmia?
options: Abnormal automaticity of a depolarised Purkinje focus
Triggered activity due to delayed afterdepolarisations (DADs)
Triggered activity due to early afterdepolarisations (EADs)
commentaires: Incorrect: abnormal automaticity does not explain the link with bradycardia and QT prolongation on sotalol.
Incorrect: scar-related re-entry causes monomorphic VT, not torsades triggered by a long QT.
Incorrect: DADs occur after repolarisation, with calcium overload, and are favoured by tachycardia, not bradycardia.
Correct: EADs arise during a prolonged action potential (bradycardia, IKr block) and trigger the initiating premature beat of torsades.
ep-meca-009.explication: Early afterdepolarisations arise during phase 2 or 3 of a prolonged action potential, notably through reactivation of the L-type calcium current. They are favoured by bradycardia, pauses, hypokalaemia and anything that prolongs repolarisation (IKr blockers such as sotalol). They trigger the initiating premature beat of torsades, which is then sustained by dispersion of repolarisation. DADs occur after full repolarisation, with calcium overload, and are favoured by tachycardia. Hence the management: magnesium, increasing the heart rate (isoprenaline or pacing) and withdrawal of the drug.
ep-meca-009.aRetenir: EADs = bradycardia + long QT → torsades; DADs = calcium overload + tachycardia.

ep-meca-010.question: Which arrhythmias are classically attributed to triggered activity due to delayed afterdepolarisations (DADs)? (multiple answers)
options: Monomorphic VT related to myocardial infarction scar
Torsades de pointes in acquired long QT
commentaires: Correct: inhibition of the Na/K pump leads to calcium overload and DADs.
Incorrect: post-infarction monomorphic VT is due to re-entry around and through the scar.
Correct: these idiopathic VTs are cAMP-dependent and driven by calcium overload; adenosine terminates them.
Incorrect: torsades de pointes are due to early afterdepolarisations (EADs), linked to prolonged repolarisation.
ep-meca-010.explication: DADs occur after repolarisation is complete, when the sarcoplasmic reticulum spontaneously releases calcium: the Na/Ca exchanger then generates a depolarising inward current. This is the mechanism of digitalis toxicity (Na/K pump inhibition and calcium overload), of CPVT (RYR2 or CASQ2 mutations) and of idiopathic outflow tract VTs, which are cAMP-dependent and typically terminated by adenosine. DADs are favoured by catecholamines and tachycardia, hence the induction of these VTs by isoprenaline or exercise. Torsades de pointes are due to early afterdepolarisations, linked to prolonged repolarisation, and post-infarction monomorphic VT to scar-related re-entry.
ep-meca-010.aRetenir: Digitalis, CPVT and adenosine-sensitive outflow tract VT = DADs (calcium overload).

ep-meca-011.question: True or false: a re-entrant tachycardia can typically be initiated and terminated reproducibly by programmed extrastimuli, whereas a tachycardia due to abnormal automaticity cannot.
commentaires: Correct: re-entry depends on unidirectional block and a critical delay that an extrastimulus can create or break; an automatic focus is merely suppressed by overdrive.
Incorrect: the statement is true; reproducible initiation and termination by programmed stimulation are the hallmark of re-entry.
ep-meca-011.explication: This is true. Reproducible initiation and termination by programmed stimulation are the hallmark of re-entry (and, to a lesser extent, of some DAD-mediated triggered activity, whose initiation is rate-dependent). An automatic focus is neither initiated nor terminated by an extrastimulus: at best it can be transiently suppressed by faster pacing (overdrive suppression) before gradually resuming. It is often unmasked by isoprenaline and shows gradual onset ("warm-up") and terminal slowing ("cool-down"). This reasoning guides the EP study and ablation strategy.
ep-meca-011.aRetenir: Reproducible initiation and termination by programmed stimulation = re-entry, not automaticity.

ep-meca-012.question: What is the "excitable gap" of a re-entrant circuit, and what is its practical relevance in electrophysiology?
ep-meca-012.reponseAttendue: The portion of tissue that has recovered excitability between the refractory tail of the preceding wavefront and the head of the next one; it allows an external stimulus to penetrate the circuit and thus to reset, entrain or terminate the tachycardia by pacing (the basis of entrainment and ATP).
ep-meca-012.explication: In anatomical re-entry (atrial flutter, scar-related VT, reciprocating tachycardia), the circuit length exceeds the wavelength: a fully or partially excitable zone persists between the head and the tail of the wavefront. A sufficiently early extrastimulus can penetrate it and advance the tachycardia (resetting), continuous pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia can entrain it, and even more aggressive pacing can create bidirectional block and terminate it. This is the basis of entrainment manoeuvres and of antitachycardia pacing by ICDs. In the functional "leading circle" model, by contrast, there is virtually no fully excitable gap. The pitfall: assuming that a tachycardia that cannot be entrained must be automatic, whereas a narrow gap or a distant pacing site may explain it.
ep-meca-012.aRetenir: The excitable gap allows re-entry to be reset, entrained and terminated by pacing.
